reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material for defense does not include an official Census Bureau adoption figure, so no measured adoption rate can be reported here. What the sources do show is a sector whose AI story is told mainly through procurement records and program structures rather than through survey percentages. The curated points describe decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with the Defense Innovation Unit serving as the commercial on-ramp for AI entering Department of Defense programs.

The primary evidence base is federal procurement data. Per SAM.gov, the government's own system of record for federal contract opportunities, AI-related DoD solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations are free and searchable there. SAM.gov also notes that the FPDS.gov "ezSearch" feature has been retired and that users should conduct all contract awards data searches in SAM.gov, with the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026. Per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level, and per USAspending, every federal award is downloadable, with contract spending on AI-related solutions tracing back to the Federal Procurement Data System feed.

On where vendors and money concentrate, the sources point to the Defense Innovation Unit as the place where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Per Govini, the defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Govini's page describes a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Per the Silicon Valley Defense Group, the nonprofit monitors the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and publicly maps the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space.

On analysis and intelligence, Janes describes itself as an open source defence and security intelligence provider whose experts collect information from vetted on-the-ground and industry specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors collecting data no web crawler could access. Janes says it verifies every data point against reliable, vetted sources, applies rigorous data governance and advanced technology to connect millions of data points, and peer reviews final content to meet a decision-grade intelligence standard. The curated points name Janes and Forecast International together as long-running defense analysis providers maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, and label them subscription sources.

The regulatory and risk posture appears in the material only indirectly. SAM.gov states that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that individuals viewing, reproducing, or disposing of it must protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy, and that the system is subject to monitoring. The World of AI page on government labs notes that state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and that such institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. It names the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China as its two verified government-lab entries.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a practical sequence rather than a verdict. Start with the free federal record: SAM.gov for solicitations and awards, USAspending for downloadable award data, and FPDS for transaction-level contract actions and vendor performance history. Use DIU's public project listings as the visible path by which commercial AI enters DoD programs, and treat Govini's public scorecards and the Silicon Valley Defense Group's mapping of commercial entrants as orientation on where money and vendors are concentrating. Where the sources are silent, this analysis stays silent: the excerpts report no ROI figures, no deployment counts, and no adoption percentages for defense, and none are asserted here.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page lists two organisations it classifies as government labs, each checked individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It says Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is described as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct place in the AI ecosystem because they carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and why. It adds that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. The page states that no entry was assigned by keyword, model, or inheritance from a parent company.
